entries.content_plain:
CHAPTER 33
 
De 33:1-28. The Majesty of God.

1. Moses the man of God--This was a common designation of a prophet (1Sa 2:27; 9:6), and it is here applied to Moses, when, like Jacob, he was about to deliver ministerially before his death, a prophetic benediction to Israel.
entries.reader_content_plain: 1. Moses the man of God--This was a common designation of a prophet (1Sa 2:27; 9:6), and it is here applied to Moses, when, like Jacob, he was about to deliver ministerially before his death, a prophetic benediction to Israel.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1943"/><div sID="gen2576" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1943"/><hi type="bold">2-4. The Lord came--</hi>Under a beautiful metaphor, borrowed from the dawn and progressive splendor of the sun, the Majesty of God is sublimely described as a divine light which appeared in Sinai and scattered its beams on all the adjoining region in directing Israel's march to Canaan. In these descriptions of a theophania, God is represented as coming from the south, and the allusion is in general to the thunderings and lightnings of Sinai; but other mountains in the same direction are mentioned with it. The location of Seir was on the east of the Ghor; mount Paran was either the chain on the west of the Ghor, or rather the mountains on the southern border of the desert towards the peninsula [Robinson]. (Compare <reference osisRef="Judg.5.4">Jud 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.5.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.7">Psa 68:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.3">Ha 3:3</reference>).<div eID="gen2576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2577" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ten thousands of saints--</hi>rendered by some, "with the ten thousand of Kadesh," or perhaps better still, "from Meribah" [Ewald].<div eID="gen2577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2578" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a fiery law--</hi>so called both because of the thunder and lightning which accompanied its promulgation (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.16-Exod.19.18">Ex 19:16-18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.11">De 4:11</reference>), and the fierce, unrelenting curse denounced against the violation of its precepts (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.7-2Cor.3.9">2Co 3:7-9</reference>). Notwithstanding those awe-inspiring symbols of Majesty that were displayed on Sinai, the law was really given in kindness and love (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.3">De 33:3</reference>), as a means of promoting both the temporal and eternal welfare of the people. And it was "the inheritance of the congregation of Jacob," not only from the hereditary obligation under which that people were laid to observe it, but from its being the grand distinction, the peculiar privilege of the nation. <div eID="gen2578" type="x-p"/>

2-4. The Lord came--Under a beautiful metaphor, borrowed from the dawn and progressive splendor of the sun, the Majesty of God is sublimely described as a divine light which appeared in Sinai and scattered its beams on all the adjoining region in directing Israel's march to Canaan. In these descriptions of a theophania, God is represented as coming from the south, and the allusion is in general to the thunderings and lightnings of Sinai; but other mountains in the same direction are mentioned with it. The location of Seir was on the east of the Ghor; mount Paran was either the chain on the west of the Ghor, or rather the mountains on the southern border of the desert towards the peninsula [Robinson]. (Compare Jud 5:4, 5; Psa 68:7, 8; Ha 3:3).
 
ten thousands of saints--rendered by some, "with the ten thousand of Kadesh," or perhaps better still, "from Meribah" [Ewald].
 
a fiery law--so called both because of the thunder and lightning which accompanied its promulgation (Ex 19:16-18; De 4:11), and the fierce, unrelenting curse denounced against the violation of its precepts (2Co 3:7-9). Notwithstanding those awe-inspiring symbols of Majesty that were displayed on Sinai, the law was really given in kindness and love (De 33:3), as a means of promoting both the temporal and eternal welfare of the people. And it was "the inheritance of the congregation of Jacob," not only from the hereditary obligation under which that people were laid to observe it, but from its being the grand distinction, the peculiar privilege of the nation.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1944"/><div sID="gen2579" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1944"/><hi type="bold">6. Let Reuben live, and not die--</hi>Although deprived of the honor and privileges of primogeniture, he was still to hold rank as one of the tribes of Israel. He was more numerous than several other tribes (<reference osisRef="Num.1.21">Nu 1:21</reference>; 2:11). Yet gradually he sank into a mere nomadic tribe, which had enough to do merely "to live and not die." Many eminent biblical scholars, resting on the most ancient and approved manuscripts of the Septuagint, consider the latter clause as referring to Simeon; "and Simeon, let his men be few," a reading of the text which is in harmony with other statements of Scripture respecting this tribe (<reference osisRef="Num.25.6-Num.14.1">Nu 25:6-14; 1</reference>:<reference osisRef="Num.14.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.26.14">26:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.19.1">Jos 19:1</reference>). <div eID="gen2579" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 6. Let Reuben live, and not die--Although deprived of the honor and privileges of primogeniture, he was still to hold rank as one of the tribes of Israel. He was more numerous than several other tribes (Nu 1:21; 2:11). Yet gradually he sank into a mere nomadic tribe, which had enough to do merely "to live and not die." Many eminent biblical scholars, resting on the most ancient and approved manuscripts of the Septuagint, consider the latter clause as referring to Simeon; "and Simeon, let his men be few," a reading of the text which is in harmony with other statements of Scripture respecting this tribe (Nu 25:6-14; 1:23; 26:14; Jos 19:1).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1946"/><div sID="gen2581" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1946"/><hi type="bold">8-10. of Levi he said--</hi>The burden of this blessing is the appointment of the Levites to the dignified and sacred office of the priesthood (<reference osisRef="Lev.10.11">Le 10:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.22.8">De 22:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.17.8-Deut.17.11">17:8-11</reference>), a reward for their zeal in supporting the cause of God, and their unsparing severity in chastising even their nearest and dearest relatives who had participated in the idolatry of the molten calf (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.25-Exod.32.28">Ex 32:25-28</reference>; compare Mal 2:4-6). <div eID="gen2581" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1948"/><div sID="gen2584" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1948"/><hi type="bold">13-17. of Joseph he said--</hi>The territory of this tribe, diversified by hill and dale, wood and water, would be rich in all the productions--olives, grapes, figs, &c., which are reared in a mountainous region, as well as in the grain and herbs that grow in the level fields. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1951"/><div sID="gen2588" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1951"/><hi type="bold">20-21. of Gad he said--</hi>Its possessions were larger than they would have been had they lain west of Jordan; and this tribe had the honor of being settled by Moses himself in the first portion of land conquered. In the forest region, south of the Jabbok, "he dwelt as a lion" (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.30.11">Ge 30:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.49.19">49:19</reference>). Notwithstanding, they faithfully kept their engagement to join the "heads of the people" [De 33:21] in the invasion of Canaan. <div eID="gen2588" type="x-p"/>
